column5: guided road to a household
column6: Abraham’s servant says YHWH led him by the right road to his master’s kin; this gives the commentary’s pairing of showing a road and its destination a literal travel scene.

column5: cloud and fire go before Israel
column6: YHWH leads the people through the wilderness with a column before them; the route is a community following its guide.

column5: God goes ahead to find a camp
column6: The verse says God went before Israel on the way and sought a place to camp, joining precedence with the destination of rest.

column5: ark precedes the travelers
column6: The ark goes ahead for three days to seek a resting place for Israel, closely matching a guide who leads a group toward where the road ends.

column5: ark leads on an unfamiliar way
column6: Israel is told to follow the ark so it can know which way to go, since it has not passed that way before; guidance makes an unknown route traversable.

column5: messenger sent ahead on the way
column6: God sends a messenger before Israel to guard them on the road and bring them to a prepared place, combining the guide’s precedence with a known destination.

column5: wanderers cannot find a dwelling city
column6: The travelers lose their way in the wilderness and find no city to live in; this makes the commentary’s image of failing to find both road and home concrete.

column5: God leads to a city by a straight way
column6: After wandering, the travelers are led on a straight route to an inhabited city; road, guidance, straightness, and home converge in one verse.

column5: ancient road and a walkable good way
column6: At a crossroads the people are told to ask for old paths, find the good way, and walk in it; the inherited road has already been trodden and must be continued.

column5: road markers and guideposts
column6: The returning people are told to set up waymarks and guideposts on the highway home; this is a direct counterpart to signs that help a traveler recover direction.

column5: blind travelers led on unknown paths
column6: God promises to lead the blind by paths they do not know, turn darkness to light, and smooth rough places; the text reverses being lost and unable to proceed.

column5: highway where travelers do not stray
column6: The holy highway leads the redeemed toward Zion, and even a fool will not lose the way; the route supplies the destination and protects against the commentary’s lost traveler.

column5: voice identifies the way and forbids turns
column6: A voice tells the traveler, “This is the way; walk in it,” when turning right or left; it makes guidance an ongoing correction against leaving the route.

column5: shepherd leads on righteous paths
column6: The shepherd leads the speaker along paths of righteousness, joining a guide who goes ahead with the communal and ethical road in the commentary.

column5: showing and teaching the paths
column6: The speaker asks God to make the divine ways known and teach the paths; this is a direct prayer for the commentary’s first movement, having the route shown.

column5: being led along the way
column6: The speaker asks God to lead him in truth; it adds active guidance to the commentary’s request to be taken along a known route.

column5: light leads to the divine dwelling
column6: The speaker asks for light and truth to lead him to the holy mountain and dwelling; a guiding marker and the road’s destination meet in one prayer.

column5: lamp at the feet and light on the path
column6: The divine word illuminates the traveler’s feet and path, a concrete scriptural image for signs that allow a person to keep direction.

column5: God makes paths straight
column6: The promise that God will make the paths straight connects acknowledgment of God with a route made traversable and direct.

column5: do not turn right or left
column6: The instruction is to keep one’s foot from evil and not swerve to either side; it gives the commentary’s straight line and refusal to deviate an ethical form.

column5: leaving upright paths for darkness
column6: These people abandon upright paths and walk in dark ways; the contrast supplies a specific scriptural picture of turning away from the straight route.

column5: apparently right way ends in death
column6: A way that seems right leads to death; the destination tests the apparent route, complementing the commentary’s insistence that knowing a way includes knowing where it leads.

column5: lost sheep and a search for return
column6: The speaker calls himself a straying sheep and asks God to seek him; this is a close image of a lost traveler needing the guide to bring him back.

column5: each sheep turns to its own way
column6: All the people have gone astray, each turning to a separate way; the verse links losing the route with communal dispersal.

column5: lost sheep, misleading shepherds, forgotten fold
column6: Israel is pictured as lost sheep whose shepherds turned them aside until they forgot their fold; wrong guidance ends in losing both route and home.

column5: scattered sheep on mountains without a shepherd
column6: The flock wanders over mountains and hills and is scattered because no one searches for it; this supplies a concrete communal counterpart to dispersion and lost direction.

column5: two paths and their different ends
column6: The Lord knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes; the verse makes a community’s road a moral course with distinct outcomes.

column5: Hebrew עבד and Arabic ع ب د
column6: The Arabic root label ع ب د belongs to the commentary, while the Hebrew verb עבד here means serving God; the cognate appears in a verse that also commands walking in God’s ways.

column5: serving God joined to walking in his ways
column6: The verse places wholehearted service beside walking in all God’s ways, giving the commentary’s worship-as-a-walked path a direct ethical counterpart.

column5: Aramaic דִּינָא in the judgment scene
column6: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن; Daniel’s Aramaic cognate appears as the court sits for judgment and the books open, grounding the judgment sense associated with the Day of Reckoning.

column5: nations taught divine paths and walking together
column6: Many peoples come to learn God’s ways and walk in them; the route is explicitly a shared path of a gathered community.

column5: leading the people to a holy abode
column6: The song says God led the redeemed people toward the dwelling-place of holiness, joining guidance to arrival at a home.

column5: Raphael knows the road and guides Tobias
column6: Tobias seeks a companion who knows the route, and Raphael offers to go because he knows the roads; this is a literal guide-and-traveler scene.

column5: cloud seen over the mountain as a sign
column6: The midrash reads Abraham’s distant sight of Moriah as a cloud attached to the mountain; it makes the destination visible as a waymark during the journey.

column5: star goes ahead and stops at the destination
column6: The star leads the travelers in front of them and stops over the place of the child; it joins a celestial sign, a guide’s precedence, and arrival.

column5: shepherd walks ahead of the sheep
column6: The shepherd goes before the flock and the sheep follow his voice, matching the commentary’s guide defined by leading from the front.

column5: the Father’s house as the destination
column6: Jesus speaks of many dwelling places in his Father’s house and says he goes to prepare a place; this makes the destination part of knowing the way.

column5: Thomas does not know the way to the destination
column6: Thomas says they do not know where Jesus is going and therefore cannot know the way; the exchange dramatizes the commentary’s link between route knowledge and knowing the house.

column5: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
column6: The destination is the Father, while Jesus calls himself the way to it; this is a Christian formulation in which the guide and route are one.

column5: guiding feet into the way of peace
column6: The hymn says the dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, directly joining a guide, bodily walking, and a named route.

column5: a broad road leads to destruction
column6: The broad entrance and road lead to destruction; it gives the commentary’s contrast between a single right path and ways that end elsewhere a specific image.

column5: a narrow way leads to life
column6: The narrow way leads to life and few find it, pairing a difficult route with its destination and the people who find it.

column5: following the light prevents walking in darkness
column6: Jesus says the follower will not walk in darkness but have the light of life; this ties following a guide to avoiding the lost traveler’s darkness.

column5: shepherd searches for a sheep that strayed
column6: The shepherd goes after the one lost sheep until he finds it; this is a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s person who has lost the way.

column5: straying sheep return to their shepherd
column6: The readers were straying like sheep and have now returned to the shepherd and guardian; the route from loss to restored guidance is explicit.

column5: forsaking the straight way for error
column6: The false teachers leave the straight way and go astray after Balaam; it directly depicts abandoning the route and its ethical course.

column5: a wanderer is turned back from error
column6: A person who wanders from the truth is brought back by another; the passage gives the commentary’s companions calling the lost traveler a communal form.

column5: the followers are called people of the Way
column6: Saul seeks those who belong to the Way; the path is the name of a community, not merely an individual direction.

column5: a traveler asks for someone to guide him
column6: On the road, the Ethiopian says he cannot understand without a guide, and Philip joins him to interpret the text; this makes guidance both travel and instruction.

column5: Jesus enters ahead as a forerunner
column6: Jesus goes into the sanctuary as a forerunner on behalf of others; the text directly connects precedence with leading people toward a destination.

column5: shepherd separates people at judgment
column6: At the Son of Man’s judgment, people are separated as a shepherd divides sheep from goats; this adds the day’s sorting of communities to the commentary’s divided paths.

column5: judgment accounts for deeds done in life
column6: All appear before the judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, connecting the commentary’s Day of Reckoning with a person’s lived course.

column5: Abraham obeys without knowing the destination
column6: Hebrews says Abraham set out without knowing where he was going; this counterpoint qualifies the commentary’s image of guidance that includes knowing the road’s destination, since faithful following can precede that knowledge.

column5: prepare a straight road in the wilderness
column6: Mark applies the call to prepare the Lord’s way and make paths straight; the route is cleared for the Lord’s arrival, adding a preparatory road to the commentary’s walkable path.

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The teaching opens by distinguishing a way of life from a way of death; it places the commentary’s contrast between the guided path and its opposite in early Christian moral instruction.

column5: two ways of light and darkness
column6: Barnabas describes two ways, light and darkness, under different authorities; this makes the competing routes a community’s ethical and spiritual allegiance.

column5: two spirits and opposing courses
column6: The Community Rule assigns people to opposing spirits and ways of righteousness or perversity; it gives the commentary’s favored community versus those led astray a sectarian map of competing routes.

column5: one perilous passage to the inherited city
column6: Ezra’s angel explains that reaching the city requires passing through a narrow way between dangers; the destination is accessible only by the difficult route.

column5: God chooses a longer route to avoid return
column6: God does not lead Israel by the nearest road because danger might make them turn back to Egypt; the chosen path is a concrete route shaped to keep travelers on course.

column5: walking God’s way as sustained practice
column6: Israel is told to keep God’s commandments and walk in his ways; this gives the commentary’s secondary image of a route maintained through repeated conduct a covenant setting.

column5: walking in God’s ways leads to life
column6: The command to love God and walk in his ways is joined to living and flourishing; it makes the moral route a practiced choice with consequences.

column5: walking, standing, and sitting as a settled pattern
column6: The verse traces a person’s association with wicked counsel from walking to standing to sitting; it gives the commentary’s secondary sense of a route as a gradually settled pattern.

column5: path of life and its destination
column6: God makes known the path of life, whose endpoint is joy in God’s presence; this is a specific path-and-destination image without a guide walking ahead.

column5: walking in the midst of paths of justice
column6: Wisdom says she walks in the way of righteousness, in the midst of paths of justice; the wording offers a concrete counterpart to the commentary’s road-center image.

column5: keeping to the way without turning aside
column6: Job says his foot has held to God’s steps and he has kept the way without turning aside; it links following a track with continued fidelity.

column5: teach me your way so I can walk in truth
column6: The prayer asks God to teach the way and unite the speaker’s heart to serve God; it joins route instruction to worshipful commitment.

column5: God alone guides the people
column6: The song says the Lord alone led Israel, with no foreign god beside him; it gives the favored community a single guide for its journey.

column5: the household must keep the way of the Lord
column6: Abraham is chosen to direct his descendants to keep the Lord’s way by doing justice and righteousness; the road is transmitted through a community and its practice.

column5: straight highway prepared through the wilderness
column6: A voice calls for a way to be prepared and a highway made straight in the desert; the relation is the route-clearing image, though this verse emphasizes preparation for God’s coming.

column5: Isaiah’s straight-way call applied to the Lord’s arrival
column6: Mark uses the wilderness highway text to frame John’s preparation of the Lord’s way; it makes the route a communal expectation of arrival.

column5: sheep distressed and scattered without a shepherd
column6: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image links a scattered people with the need for a guide, though it does not itself describe their road.

column5: hearts that continually go astray
column6: The wilderness generation is described as always going astray in heart and not knowing God’s ways; the passage links lost direction with failure to know the divine route.

column5: Christ as the way to the Father
column6: Augustine reads Jesus’s “I am the way” as Christ himself mediating access to the Father; this interprets the route-and-destination relation as a person rather than a road.

column5: two moral ways and inclinations
column6: The testament contrasts good and evil ways and the dispositions that choose them; it is a specific Jewish two-route parallel, though its verse divisions vary between editions.

column5: he heavenly lights serve as signs
column6: Genesis assigns the lights signs for seasons and days, not route guidance; this is a limited counterpart to the commentary’s stars as travelers’ markers and keeps the two uses distinct.

column5: staff carried through a dangerous valley
column6: The speaker’s rod and staff comfort him while walking through the valley, a concrete staff-on-the-road image; the verse does not say the staff goes ahead as the commentary’s gloss does.
